source.title: Recent advances in open billiards with some open problems

accepted.question_text: Let Φ^t: Ω → Ω be an open dynamical system, with t discrete for maps and continuous for flows, and let H ⊂ Ω be a hole through which trajectories are absorbed. For an initial measure μ0, let Ω_t be the survivor set of points whose trajectories do not enter H during (0,t], let P(t)=μ0(Ω_t) be the survival probability, and let γ be the exponential escape rate when it exists. If μ∞ is a conditionally invariant limiting survivor measure and ν is the natural invariant measure on the repeller, how generally does the escape-rate formula γ = sum of the positive Lyapunov exponents minus the Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy h_KS, with the quantities computed with respect to ν, remain valid, especially beyond uniformly hyperbolic maps and for flows?

evidence.quote: The conditionally invariant measure μ∞ is supported on the set of points with infinite past avoiding the hole
Pesin’s formula generalises in the open case to the “escape rate formula” [28, 37] γ = ∑ i:λi>0 λi − hKS (6) where the quantities on the right hand side are defined with respect to ν.
Open problem 1. How general is the escape rate formula, Eq. (6)?

accepted.question_text: For sufficiently chaotic billiard models with a small hole H of relative size h and escape rate γ, can one prove a local escape-rate formula analogous to the known formulas for piecewise expanding maps, in which γ/h has a limit as the hole shrinks to a point and the limiting value reflects whether the limiting point is periodic and the stability of that periodic point?

evidence.quote: In [18, 47] it is shown that γ/h can reach a limit, the local escape rate, as the hole shrinks to a point, and that the limit depends on whether the point is periodic.
Open problem 2. Local escape rate: Proof of a formula similar to Eq. (7) for sufficiently chaotic billiard models.

accepted.question_text: In open dynamical systems, including billiards with distortion, nonuniform hyperbolicity, or no hyperbolicity, how should the position of a hole be chosen in order to maximize or minimize escape, where the measure of escape may be the escape rate γ, the full survival probability function P(t), or another suitably defined escape statistic?

evidence.quote: Another important question posed in this work is that of optimisation: how to choose a hole position to minimise or maximise escape, for example γ or even the whole function P(t) [1, 18].
Open problem 3. Optimisation: Specify where to place a hole to maximise or minimise a suitably defined measure of escape.

accepted.question_text: For a family of open billiards with a variable hole H, let h=|H|/|M| be the hole size relative to the billiard boundary phase space M, and let P(t)=μ0(Ω_t) be the survival probability at time t for an initial measure μ0. For which billiards, and in which joint limits of long time t and small hole size h, does P(t) reduce to a function only of the product h t?

evidence.quote: what is the probability P(t) = μ0(Ωt) that the particle survives until time t? How does this probability behave as a function of t, the initial measure μ0, the hole location H, its size relative to the billiard boundary h = |H|/|M|
If instead both limits are taken simultaneously so that ht is constant, the survival probability numerically appears to reach a limiting function.
Open problem 4. Scaling: For what billiards and in what limits does P(t) reduce to a function of ht for a family of billiards with variable hole size h?

accepted.question_text: Does every triangular billiard contain at least one periodic orbit, and more generally does every polygonal billiard contain at least one periodic orbit when arbitrary directions of motion are allowed?

evidence.quote: Open problem 5. Existence of periodic orbits: Do all triangular (or more generally polygonal) billiards contain at least one periodic orbit?
Note that this admits arbitrary directions; it is easy to construct rational polygonal billiards for which a particular directional flow is never periodic.

accepted.question_text: Can a polygonal billiard be mixing, necessarily in a case with at least one irrational angle, given that rational polygonal billiards are typically ergodic in fixed-direction restrictions but not mixing and irrational-angle polygonal billiards cannot have positive Lyapunov exponents?

evidence.quote: Very little is known about the case of irrational angles [43, 70], except that usual characteristics of chaoticity such as positive Lyapunov exponents are not possible here.
Open problem 6. Mixing property: Is it possible for a polygonal billiard (necessarily with at least one irrational angle) to be mixing?

accepted.question_text: In open polygonal billiards, is the asymptotic survival probability P(t) as t tends to infinity entirely determined by neighborhoods of non-escaping periodic orbits?

evidence.quote: In [30] it was found numerically that P(t) decayed as C/t in an irrational polygonal billiard where at least one periodic orbit was present, and vanished at finite time in a directional flow for a rational polygonal billiard containing no periodic orbits.
Open problem 7. Is the asymptotic survival probability P(t) as t → ∞ in polygonal billiards entirely determined by the neighbourhoods of non-escaping periodic orbits?

accepted.question_text: For dispersing billiards with small holes, can one give a rigorous formulation of the proposed small-hole escape-rate expansion in which the exponential escape rate, including the differential escape rate for two holes A and B, is expressed through a series of correlation functions of zero-mean phase functions associated with the holes under the billiard collision map F?

evidence.quote: the exponential escape rate γ as above can be expanded in powers of the hole size h using series of correlation functions, as can the differential escape rate of one vs two holes.
Open problem 8. Give a rigorous formulation of the escape rate of dispersing billiards with small holes along the lines of Eq. (9).

accepted.question_text: For stadium-like billiards containing marginally unstable periodic orbits, can one comprehensively characterize their dynamical properties, including escape properties, in terms of reinjection dynamics, meaning the way trajectories that leave the neighborhood of such periodic orbits are returned to that neighborhood?
accepted.context_brief: reinjection near marginally unstable periodic orbits

evidence.quote: One source of interest and also difficulty with the stadium is the fact that orbits that leave the bouncing ball region are immediately reinjected back

Open problem 9. Give a comprehensive characterisation of the dynamical (including escape) properties of marginally unstable periodic orbits in stadium-like billiards in terms of their reinjection dynamics.

accepted.question_text: Is there a universal decay rate for the long-time survival probability in generic open billiards with mixed phase space, where typical trajectories may be regular or chaotic depending on initial condition and sticky motion near elliptic islands is conjectured in area-preserving maps to produce algebraic survival decay with a universal exponent?

evidence.quote: Typical billiards are expected to have mixed phase space, that is, chaotic or regular depending on the initial condition
Open problem 10. Is there a universal decay rate in generic open billiards?

accepted.question_text: In mushroom billiards and similar mixed-phase-space billiards, how can one characterize escape at the boundary between regular and chaotic regions, including the possible slowing of survival decay by sticky marginally unstable periodic orbits and by the regular-chaotic boundary itself when the hole lies in the chaotic region?

evidence.quote: The decay of the survival probability in the case that the hole is in the chaotic region may be significantly slowed both by stickiness due to marginally unstable periodic orbits, and by the boundary itself.
Open problem 11. Characterise the escape properties of the boundary between regular and chaotic regions in mushroom and similar billiards.

accepted.question_text: For many-particle physical systems whose dynamics is predominantly chaotic, how prevalent are regular regions of phase space, such as elliptic islands, and how important are those regions for the system's dynamics and physical behavior?

evidence.quote: A system of many particles undergoing hard collisions corresponds to a high dimensional billiard.
Open problem 12. For physical systems with many particles which are predominantly chaotic, how prevalent and important are the regular regions (“elliptic islands”) in phase space?

accepted.question_text: For billiard-like models used in statistical mechanics, including Lorentz gases with infinitely many convex scatterers and Ehrenfest gases with infinitely many polygons, what minimum microscopic dynamical properties are required to obtain a chaotic macroscopic limit, such as recurrence, ergodicity, a normal diffusion coefficient, or convergence to a limiting Wiener diffusion process?

evidence.quote: Low-dimensional billiards imitating hard-ball motion are popular for understanding statistical mechanics, particularly Lorentz gases consisting of an infinite number of convex (typically circular) scatterers and the Ehrenfest gases consisting of an infinite number of polygons
Open problem 13. What are minimum dynamical properties required for a “chaotic” macroscopic limit, for example recurrence, ergodicity, a “normal” diffusion coefficient, a limiting Weiner process?

accepted.question_text: What experimental techniques can best probe the limits of statistical mechanics that arise from two preceding issues: how regular elliptic-island regions matter in predominantly chaotic many-particle systems, and what minimum microscopic dynamical properties are needed for chaotic macroscopic limits such as recurrence, ergodicity, normal diffusion, or limiting Wiener behavior?

evidence.quote: Open problem 12. For physical systems with many particles which are predominantly chaotic, how prevalent and important are the regular regions (“elliptic islands”) in phase space?
Open problem 13. What are minimum dynamical properties required for a “chaotic” macroscopic limit, for example recurrence, ergodicity, a “normal” diffusion coefficient, a limiting Weiner process?
Open problem 14. What experimental techniques might best probe the limits of statistical mechanics arising from the previous two open problems?

accepted.question_text: For an open quantum billiard, modeled by the Helmholtz equation (∇^2 + k^2)ψ = 0 with Dirichlet boundary conditions and resonance solutions whose wavenumber k has negative imaginary part, is the number of resonant states with Re(k_n) < k and Im(k_n) > -C for a positive constant C of order k^(d_H+1) as k tends to infinity, where d_H is the partial Hausdorff dimension of the classical non-escaping set?

evidence.quote: If the billiard is open, for example consisting of a finite region containing obstacles that do not prevent the particle escaping to infinity, the Helmholtz equation has resonance solutions where k has negative imaginary part.

Open problem 15. The fractal Weyl conjecture: The number of states with Re(kn) < k and Im(kn) > −C for some positive constant C is of order k dH+1 where again k → ∞ and dH is the partial Hausdorff dimension of the non-escaping set.

accepted.question_text: How can billiard models be generalized to include more realistic physical effects, such as soft wall potentials, external fields, dissipative or stochastic scattering at the boundary or in the interior, and time-dependent boundaries, while retaining mathematical or physical interest as models of open dynamical systems?

evidence.quote: Open problem 16. Generalisations: Billiards with more realistic physical effects, for example soft wall potentials, external fields, dissipative and/or stochastic scattering (at the boundary or in the interior) or time dependent boundaries.
The possibilities are endless; for this reason, it is increasingly important to carefully justify the mathematical and/or physical interest of any new model.

accepted.question_text: For a given open or generalized billiard system, can the survival probability P(t) be expressed exactly, or at least expanded for large time t beyond the leading asymptotic term, particularly in well-understood cases such as integrable and dispersing billiards?

evidence.quote: Open problem 17. Exact expansions: For a given open (generalised) billiard problem, can the survival probability P(t) be expressed exactly, or at least as an expansion for large t that goes beyond the leading term?
The most likely candidates for this problem are those billiards that are best understood, the integrable and dispersing cases.

accepted.question_text: For open dynamical systems with little or no hyperbolicity, how does recurrence affect escape, including the influence of periodic orbits and more general recurrent structures both near the hole and elsewhere in phase space, on escape rates, non-escaping sets, and long-time survival behavior?

evidence.quote: Periodic orbits denote an exact recurrence to the initial state of a classical system, and so contribute directly to the set of orbits that enter from a hole and return there after one period.

Open problem 18. Recurrence: Give a general description of how the escape problem is affected by recurrences in the system (periodic orbits or more general), in the vicinity of the hole and/or elsewhere, for systems with little or no hyperbolicity.

accepted.question_text: From escape measurements in a billiard system, what information can be recovered about the billiard dynamics, and can escape data determine or reveal the shape of the underlying billiard domain in an analogue of asking whether one can hear the shape of a drum?

evidence.quote: Finally, a question posed in [15] but for which a systematic solution does not appear to exist in the literature:
Open problem 19. Inverse problems: What information can be extracted about the dynamics of a billiard from escape measurements? Can you “peep” the shape of a drum?

Local shard metadata identified the exact work as 'Recent advances in open billiards with some open problems' and exposed exact-work links to DOI 10.1142/9789814340700_0011 and arXiv abs 1007.4166. The arXiv landing page title and PDF title confirmed the same work; the arXiv PDF was used as the readable primary source. Shell curl to api.zbmath.org failed with network_or_dns_failure in this environment, so zbMATH/API metadata was not used for extraction.
